newsitem.title: UK: LME copper nudges the highs, aluminium follows.
newsitem.headline: LME copper nudges the highs, aluminium follows.

text.p: Copper prices finished close to the day's highs on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday, driven by another fall in stocks and global supply tightness.
Aluminium followed higher in late dealings, nickel recovered from Monday's two year lows and lead pared some of the early fund-driven losses.
LME stocks fell below 100,000 tonnes for the first time since 1990 when a net 5,050 tonnes moved out on Tuesday.
Three month futures responded by closing the afternoon kerb session $66 higher at $2,225 a tonne, not far from the five-month high of $2,232 hit earlier in the day.

"Copper has the potential to push higher, with stocks falling and spreads tightening," said Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff. But with technical indicators now heavily overbought a short term correction lower was needed, he added.
Support was pegged at $2,185 and $2,150 while resistance was expected to emerge at $2,280.
Cash widened to around $155 above three month values from $118 at Monday's close. Cash/day was last indicated at around level against a small $2 backwardation on Monday, traders said.
Aluminium pushed higher, spurred on by copper's strength and a slight tightening in nearby spreads.
"Things are starting to get tight on aluminium," said Squires. Tuesday's stock drawdown of 2,825 tonnes was also supportive, he added.

Three month futures finished $29.50 higher at $1,464 but continued to rally after the kerb to $1,485 bid at 1735 GMT. This took the market above a long-term downtrend extending back to August 1995, chartists said.
Traders noted forward buying on futures and options, which some said was also helping lift values.
Prices have not been this high since early September.
Nickel recovered from two-year lows posted on Monday.
Stocks rose 468 tonnes, but short-covering and trade buying reversed some of Monday's declines. The market ended $240 higher at $6,860, with $7,000 seen as major resistance.

Lead fell sharply in early trade, knocked by fund liquidation after a long term rising trendline was broken. Values managed to recover back above $700 by the close, but at $703 the market was still off $14.50.
Battery producers were expected to enter the market and buy physical metal if the market dropped much further, traders said.
Zinc rose moderately to $1,062 from $1,058 after stocks fell 650 tonnes.
Tin gained $10 to $6,040 after stocks fell 85 tonnes.
Alloy was last indicated at $1,320/25 from $1,300/05. Stocks fell 260 tonnes.
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
